full_text:
great question

what matters is real yield

if real yield is what drives incentives, and it ends up at zero in bith scenarios, then the deciding factor should be whichever scenario makes ETH a harder money

if real yield terminates at the same value in either scenario (zero, or slightly negative) ETH is a harder money in the scenario where nominal yield is lower, even though real yield remains the same

appreciation to ETH as an asset is a much stronger source of “income” for stakers than staking yield anyways, so we should bias the scenario that makes ETH harder money
name: Evan 🦇🔊

full_text:
> what matters is real yield 
Not as much as you think when it comes to decentralisation. 95%+ of the validator set aren’t only running their own eth. Meaning almost all of our existing stake diversity is not experiencing this dilution (on a significant portion of their stake). 
RPL operators, CSM operators, all the long tail staking are making a significant amount of their rewards on their fee cut on the delegated eth. 

On the centralised side my point is (unfortunately) stronger, these entities put no capital down, so they are not experiencing dilution almost at all (unless they hold eth, but that’s a fraction of what they stake)

> we should bias to the scenario that makes eth harder money. 

If issuance was like the PoW days, I’d agree with you. Sub 1%, I think Eth’s monetary premium from being very decentralised is larger than its premium for being ‘hard money’ (changing issuance in the first place does a sizeable blow to the hard money narrative for a number of years)
